92: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.70, with a coefficient of variation of 0.73 per cent.
94: The probable basis of the differences in predicted glycaemic index is that the rate of starch hydrolysis, rather than the total quantity of starch, determines the glycaemic response of a cereal food (Jenkins et al., 1981; Goni et al., 1997). The carrot fortified treatments returned the lowest values because the dietary fibre of carrot forms a physical barrier around the starch granule and retards the access of pancreatic amylase, and because these treatments also carried the highest resistant starch (Sajilata et al., 2006; Sharma et al., 2012; Slavin, 2013). The beet fortified treatments returned the highest values because beetroot supplies a large quantity of free sugars absorbed almost immediately (Singh and Hathan, 2014; Chhikara et al., 2019). Frei et al. (2003) and Panlasigui et al. (1991) both demonstrated for rice that varieties of comparable amylose content may differ widely in starch digestibility and glycaemic response, which accounts for the failure of the treatment ranking here to follow amylose alone. The values obtained fall within the intermediate to high range of the international tables of Foster-Powell et al. (2002).
105: Total soluble protein (Table 4.8 and Fig. 4.8) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in KBI (2.71 per cent), followed by RBI (2.54 per cent), and lowest in DI (1.05 per cent). Among the products the mean value was 2.23 in the beet fortified product, 2.05 in the carrot fortified product and 1.27 in the plain product. Among the varieties it was highest in Kalojira (1.98) and lowest in Dudeshwar (1.71).
106: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.04, with a coefficient of variation of 1.96 per cent.
108: The most probable basis of the rise in total soluble protein on fortification is the proteolysis accompanying natural lactic fermentation together with the soluble protein contributed by the vegetable extract. During the overnight leavening of the batter, the proteases of Leuconostoc and Lactobacillus species hydrolyse a proportion of the rice and black gram protein into soluble peptides and free amino nitrogen, which are recovered in the Folin-Ciocalteu assay of Lowry et al. (1951) but not in the intact protein (Mukherjee et al., 1965; Chavan and Kadam, 1989; Soni and Sandhu, 1990). Ghosh and Chattopadhyay (2011) measured this increase directly in idli batter and reported a marked rise in soluble nitrogen during fermentation, and comparable increases have been recorded in other fermented cereal systems (Blandino et al., 2003; Poutanen et al., 2009). Beetroot likewise carries readily extractable protein of its own, which accounts for the beet fortified treatments ranking highest for this character (Singh and Hathan, 2014; Chhikara et al., 2019).
117: Total protein (Table 4.9 and Fig. 4.9) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in KI (13.44 per cent), followed by KBI (13.29 per cent), and lowest in DCI (10.92 per cent). Among the products the mean value was 12.83 in the plain product, 12.69 in the beet fortified product and 11.43 in the carrot fortified product. Among the varieties it was highest in Kalojira (12.87) and lowest in Dudeshwar (11.58).
118: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.08, with a coefficient of variation of 0.61 per cent.
120: The idli was considerably richer in protein than milled rice, and the most probable basis is the combined contribution of black gram and of microbial biomass. The batter contains rice and black gram in a two to one ratio, and the lysine-rich protein of black gram compensates for the lysine-deficient protein of rice, yielding a product of better amino acid balance than either component alone (Reddy et al., 1981; Ufaz and Galili, 2008; Oghbaei and Prakash, 2016). Fermentation contributes further protein through the growth of the microflora and improves its digestibility by partial proteolysis (Chavan and Kadam, 1989; Nout and Sarkar, 1999; Sridevi et al., 2010). The superiority of the three aromatic landraces over the non-aromatic check, and the combination of high protein with low amylose in Radhunipagal, accord with the negative relation between grain protein and amylose reported for rice by Chattopadhyay et al. (2018), while the general level of protein recorded is comparable with the values reported for Indian rices by Rani et al. (2006) and Gopalan et al. (2004). A comparable dominance of the grain protein in the finished product was recorded by Kaviyaselvan et al. (2026), who separated the protein of idli into its four solubility fractions and found glutelin to be the largest, followed by prolamin, globulin and albumin.
129: Fat content (Table 4.10 and Fig. 4.10) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in KI (0.28 per cent), followed by GCI (0.28 per cent), and lowest in GBI (0.17 per cent). Among the products the mean value was 0.26 in the carrot fortified product, 0.24 in the plain product and 0.19 in the beet fortified product. Among the varieties it was highest in Dudeshwar (0.25) and lowest in Gobindabhog (0.21).
130: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.04, with a coefficient of variation of 15.91 per cent.
132: Fat was uniformly low in all the treatments, the probable basis being that idli is steamed rather than fried, so that no fat is added during preparation and the only lipid present is that of the rice and black gram themselves (Reddy et al., 1981; Gopalan et al., 2004). Rice endosperm carries very little lipid once the bran has been removed, and black gram is likewise a low-fat pulse (Champagne, 2004; Oghbaei and Prakash, 2016). The marginally higher values recorded in the carrot fortified treatments are most probably an artefact of the method rather than a genuine gain in fat, since the carotenoids of carrot are lipid-soluble and are extracted along with the fat during Soxhlet extraction, where they are weighed as part of the crude fat fraction (Britton, 1995; Rodriguez-Amaya, 2001; Sharma et al., 2012). A small loss of lipid through microbial lipase activity during fermentation may contribute further to the low values overall (Blandino et al., 2003; Nout, 2009).
141: Ash content (Table 4.11 and Fig. 4.11) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in GBI (5.21 per cent), followed by GCI (4.89 per cent), and lowest in DI (2.47 per cent). Among the products the mean value was 4.35 in the beet fortified product, 3.97 in the carrot fortified product and 2.94 in the plain product. Among the varieties it was highest in Gobindabhog (4.57) and lowest in Kalojira (3.35).
142: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.24, with a coefficient of variation of 0.98 per cent.
144: Ash represents the total mineral load of the product, and the most probable basis of its rise on fortification is the direct mineral contribution of the vegetable extract. Beetroot is a rich source of potassium, sodium, calcium and magnesium, and the addition of its extract raises the inorganic residue of the product substantially (Singh and Hathan, 2014; Chhikara et al., 2019), while carrot contributes a smaller but still appreciable quantity (Sharma et al., 2012). The high ash content of Gobindabhog among the varieties is consistent with its superior mineral profile discussed in the following section and reflects a genuine varietal difference in grain mineral status (Rani et al., 2006; Hemalatha et al., 2007; Gopalan et al., 2004). Values of this order have been reported for other fermented cereal and pulse products, in which the ash content is generally higher than that of the unfermented raw material on account of the loss of dry matter as carbon dioxide during leavening (Blandino et al., 2003; Oghbaei and Prakash, 2016).
153: Phytate content (Table 4.12 and Fig. 4.12) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in KBI (2.52 mg g⁻¹), followed by RBI (2.03 mg g⁻¹), and lowest in GI (0.82 mg g⁻¹). Among the products the mean value was 1.85 in the beet fortified product, 1.49 in the carrot fortified product and 1.10 in the plain product. Among the varieties it was highest in Kalojira (1.92) and lowest in Gobindabhog (1.09).
154: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.04, with a coefficient of variation of 2.50 per cent.
156: The most probable basis of the rise in phytate on fortification is that beetroot itself contributes phytate to the batter, phytate being the principal storage form of phosphorus in plant tissues (Reddy et al., 1982; Singh and Hathan, 2014). Phytate is of consequence because the six phosphate groups of the inositol ring chelate calcium, iron and zinc in the gastrointestinal tract and form insoluble complexes that are poorly absorbed (Haug and Lantzsch, 1983; Sandberg, 2002; Hemalatha et al., 2007). It is therefore encouraging that all the values recorded here lie well below those customarily reported for raw rice and black gram. The probable reason is that phytase derived from the grain itself and from the fermenting microflora hydrolyses a large proportion of the phytate during the soaking and overnight fermentation of the batter, a reduction demonstrated in rice, wheat, sorghum and legumes alike (Lestienne et al., 2005; Hotz and Gibson, 2007; Liang et al., 2008; Gupta et al., 2015). The mineral gain conferred by fortification is thus partly offset by the accompanying rise in phytate, and the phytate to mineral molar ratio rather than the mineral content alone should be used in judging the nutritional value of the product.
167: Total phenol content (Table 4.13 and Fig. 4.13) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in KBI (290.97 mg GAE 100 g⁻¹), followed by RBI (279.83 mg GAE 100 g⁻¹), and lowest in DI (53.47 mg GAE 100 g⁻¹). Among the products the mean value was 265.23 in the beet fortified product, 152.64 in the carrot fortified product and 89.40 in the plain product. Among the varieties it was highest in Kalojira (198.14) and lowest in Dudeshwar (132.08).
168: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.66, with a coefficient of variation of 0.34 per cent.
170: Two independent sources acting in concert constitute the most probable explanation for the very wide range recorded for total phenol. The first is the parent grain: the pigmented pericarp of the black-husked Kalojira carries a large pool of phenolic acids and proanthocyanidins, and pigmented rice grains have repeatedly been shown to contain several times more phenolics than white grains (Zhang et al., 2010; Sompong et al., 2011; Shao et al., 2014; Goufo and Trindade, 2014). The second is the fortifying material: beetroot supplies betalains together with an appreciable quantity of phenolic acids, and these compounds are reasonably stable at the mildly acidic pH generated by lactic fermentation and survive the brief moist heat of steaming (Kanner et al., 2001; Ravichandran et al., 2013; Chhikara et al., 2019). Fermentation itself may make a third and smaller contribution, since microbial esterases liberate bound phenolic acids from the cell wall matrix and render them extractable, an effect demonstrated in rice, barley and oat systems (Dordevic et al., 2010; Hole et al., 2012; Ti et al., 2014). The superiority of the aromatic landraces over the non-aromatic check likewise accords with the comparison made by Ghosh and Roychoudhury (2018). Kaviyaselvan et al. (2026) separated the phenolics of idli into soluble free, soluble bound and insoluble bound forms and found the insoluble bound fraction to be the largest and the pigmented formulations consistently richer than the non-pigmented ones, which supports the varietal effect recorded here.
179: Total flavonoid content (Table 4.14 and Fig. 4.14) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in KBI (171.34 mg QE 100 g⁻¹), followed by GBI (152.14 mg QE 100 g⁻¹), and lowest in DI (42.95 mg QE 100 g⁻¹). Among the products the mean value was 142.75 in the beet fortified product, 89.52 in the carrot fortified product and 60.37 in the plain product. Among the varieties it was highest in Kalojira (115.54) and lowest in Dudeshwar (73.54).
180: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.60, with a coefficient of variation of 0.54 per cent.
182: The probable basis of the flavonoid pattern is the same as that of total phenol, the two fractions sharing a common origin and comparable extraction behaviour. Flavonoids in cereal grains are concentrated in the bran, aleurone and pericarp layers, which are best developed and most heavily pigmented in the black-husked Kalojira (Adom and Liu, 2002; Liu, 2007; Sompong et al., 2011; Goufo and Trindade, 2014). Beetroot supplies a further quantity through its betalain and flavonoid fraction (Kanner et al., 2001; Chhikara et al., 2019), and carrot contributes a smaller amount (Sharma et al., 2012). The release of bound flavonoids from the cell wall matrix by microbial enzymes during fermentation constitutes a probable additional contribution, as has been demonstrated for several fermented cereals (Dordevic et al., 2010; Hole et al., 2012; Ti et al., 2014). The identical ranking of the treatments for phenol and flavonoid supports the interpretation that both were governed by the same two sources. The same order was recorded by Kaviyaselvan et al. (2026) in idli prepared from pigmented rice and pearl millet, in which the insoluble bound flavonoid fraction was the largest and the pigmented formulations again exceeded the non-pigmented ones.
